Metternich. Klemens von Metternich, an Austrian statesman and diplomat whose conservative vision dominated European politics for three decades after Napoleon's defeat. As the architect of the Concert of Europe and the post-Napoleonic order, he epitomized the conservative reaction against revolution and the principle of legitimacy in international affairs.

Metternich became Austria's Foreign Minister in 1809 and chief diplomat. He negotiated alliances, marriages, and peace settlements that shaped the outcome of the Napoleonic Wars. He orchestrated the Congress of Vienna from 1814 to 1815, the peace conference that reorganized Europe after Napoleon's defeat and established the Concert of Europe system. He championed the principle of legitimacy—the restoration of pre-revolutionary dynasties and territorial boundaries—as the foundation for European stability.

He designed the Concert of Europe, a system of great-power consensus and collective security meant to prevent future revolutionary upheaval and maintain conservative order. He pursued a policy of conservative internationalism, using diplomacy, secret police, and suppression of nationalist movements to prevent the spread of revolutionary ideas. He opposed nationalist and liberal movements throughout Europe, viewing them as threats to established monarchies and the balance of power he had carefully constructed.

Metternich maintained influence over Austrian policy for nearly forty years until the revolutions of 1848 forced his resignation, demonstrating the durability but ultimate fragility of his system. His conservative order preserved great-power stability for nearly a century, but his refusal to accommodate legitimate national aspirations sowed seeds of later conflict and European instability. Metternich remains connected to the Congress of Vienna where he exerted maximum influence over European reconstruction, Napoleon Bonaparte whose defeat made his conservative order possible, Conservatism as the political ideology he embodied and promoted through international statecraft, and Austria, the empire whose interests he advanced through diplomatic skill and great-power politics.
